questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: The listed causes of thrombotic microangiopathy are HUS, HELLP syndrome, malignant hypertension and the rheumatological conditions:
opts: Catastrophic APS and systemic lupus erythematosus
questions.exp: Causes: HUS; HELLP; rheumatological condition – catastrophic APS, diffuse scleroderma; malignant hypertension. (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: The expansion of HELLP syndrome as written is:
opts: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, low plasma volume
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, low platelet
questions.exp: HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, low platelet). (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: The heading 'Rheumatological Condition' is bracketed against catastrophic APS and diffuse scleroderma, and not against HUS or HELLP.
opts: True — and the same bracket also includes Takayasu arteritis
True — only those two causes carry that label
False — HUS is also filed under rheumatological conditions
False — the label sits beside malignant hypertension
questions.exp: The causes list runs HUS, HELLP, then the rheumatological bracket over catastrophic APS and diffuse scleroderma (Anti RNA P), then malignant hypertension; Takayasu and PAN appear on the opposite side of the vessel-size comparison. (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: The antibody annotated with diffuse scleroderma in the cause list is:
questions.exp: Diffuse scleroderma (anti RNA P). (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: Match each condition with its renal-vessel category — 1) Catastrophic APS / diffuse scleroderma 2) Takayasu arteritis / polyarteritis nodosa 3) Malignant hypertension … A) Accelerated HTN + papilloedema B) Smaller vessels of kidney C) Larger vessels of kidney
questions.exp: Catastrophic APS/diffuse scleroderma involve smaller vessels of kidney v/s larger vessels (Takayasu, PAN); malignant HTN = accelerated HTN + papilloedema. (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: Malignant hypertension is defined in the book as accelerated HTN plus:
questions.exp: Malignant hypertension = accelerated HTN + papilloedema. (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: Fill up: In the malignant-hypertension note, the new onset fundal changes are written as hemorrhage/______.
questions.exp: The bracket reads: (New onset fundal changes: hemorrhage/exudate + emergency HTN: end organ damage + ≥180/120). (Book p753)

questions.sec: TMA causes & malignant hypertension · p753
questions.q: Emergency hypertension in the malignant-HTN note is end-organ damage with a BP of at least:
questions.exp: Emergency HTN: end organ damage + ≥180/120; new onset fundal changes: hemorrhage/exudate. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Fill up: The HUS triad is thrombocytopenia, renal failure and ______.
questions.exp: Triad: thrombocytopenia, renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: All of the following form the HUS triad EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Fever belongs to the TTP pentad, not the HUS triad. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Compared with the HUS triad, the TTP pentad adds fever, GI symptoms and:
questions.exp: TTP pentad: thrombocytopenia, fever, MAHA, neurological symptoms [brain], GI symptoms. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: What is written in square brackets beneath 'Neurological symptoms' in the TTP pentagon?
questions.exp: The pentagon's vertex is labelled 'Neurological Symptoms [Brain]', localising the fifth feature of the TTP pentad. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Every corner of the TTP pentagon is listed below EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The pentagon carries thrombocytopenia, fever, MAHA, neurological symptoms (brain) and GI symptoms; renal failure is the third corner of the HUS triangle, not of the pentad. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Which statement comparing the two shapes is TRUE?
opts: TTP's pentagon replaces renal failure with neurological symptoms
Both shapes list exactly the same five features
The HUS triangle is thrombocytopenia, renal failure and MAHA, while TTP's pentagon adds fever, GI and neurological symptoms
The HUS triangle includes fever while TTP's pentagon does not
questions.exp: Triad vs pentagon as drawn: TTP adds GI symptoms, fever and neurological symptoms [brain]. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Typical HUS/D+ begins in childhood, commonly below the age of:
questions.exp: Typical HUS/D+ onset: childhood, commonly age <5 years; cause: infection i.e dysentery; prognosis good. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: Atypical HUS/D- differs from typical HUS by:
opts: Childhood onset with dysentery and a good prognosis
Any-age onset, genetic (m/c) or sporadic drug-induced cause, and 50% progressing to ESRD with post-transplant recurrence
questions.exp: Atypical HUS/D-: any age; genetic (m/c)/sporadic (drug induced); bad prognosis (50% progress to ESRD); ↑ recurrence after renal transplant. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: In the TYPES table, what proportion of atypical HUS cases progress to ESRD?
questions.exp: The prognosis row for atypical HUS/D− prints 'Bad (50% progress to ESRD)' along with increased chances of recurrence after renal transplant, while typical HUS is simply 'Good'. (Book p753)

questions.sec: HUS features, TTP pentad & types · p753
questions.q: A 34-year-old with dysentery-negative HUS is counselled before a living-related transplant. Which line of the TYPES table applies to him?
opts: Typical HUS — prognosis good because the cause is infection
Neither, since the table says nothing about transplantation
Atypical HUS — any age, bad prognosis with increased recurrence after renal transplant
Typical HUS — childhood onset with good prognosis
questions.exp: The atypical column lists any-age onset, genetic (m/c) or sporadic drug-induced cause, bad prognosis with 50% progress to ESRD and increased chances of recurrence after renal transplant. (Book p753)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: The pathophysiology chain starts with endothelial damage, which next causes:
opts: VWF release and platelet plug formation
questions.exp: Endothelial damage → VWF release → platelet plug formation. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: In the pathophysiology flowchart, thrombocytopenia is reached by which route?
opts: Platelet plug formation → platelet trapped in plug
questions.exp: The diagram drops a branch from platelet plug formation: 'Platelet trapped in plug → Thrombocytopenia', running parallel to the schistocyte/MAHA limb. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Fill up: In the TMA flowchart, platelets trapped in the plug produce ______.
questions.exp: Platelet trapped in plug → thrombocytopenia. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Schistocyte formation and hence MAHA arise because:
opts: Fibrin strands are absent from the microvessels
Circulating erythrocytes are damaged by the platelet plug
Autoantibodies lyse the red cell membrane
questions.exp: Schistocyte formation d/t platelet plug circulating erythrocytes damage → MAHA. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Typical/childhood HUS accounts for what proportion of cases?
questions.exp: Typical/childhood: 90% cases, toxin driven. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: The enterohemorrhagic E. coli strain flagged as m/c is:
questions.exp: EHEC O157:H7 (m/c). (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Match each toxin with its organism — 1) Shiga like toxin / verocytotoxin 2) Shiga toxin 3) Neuraminidase toxin … A) Shigella dysentery B) Streptococcus pneumoniae C) Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7)
questions.exp: Shiga like toxin/verocytotoxin – EHEC O157:H7; Shiga toxin – Shigella dysentery; neuraminidase toxin – Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Genetic (atypical) HUS is caused by activation of the alternate complement pathway, with the complement profile:
questions.exp: A/w: low C3, normal C4. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Match each genetic type of atypical HUS with its prognostic label — 1) Complement factor-H mutation 2) Complement factor-B 3) Membrane cofactor-P (MCP) … A) Worst prognosis B) Best prognosis C) m/c mutation
questions.exp: Factor-H (m/c) mutation; factor-B worst prognosis; MCP best prognosis; factor-I also listed. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Among sporadic drug-induced HUS agents, the pair also bracketed to TTP is:
questions.exp: Ticlopidine + clopidogrel are annotated "TTP also" among drug-induced causes. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Match each sporadic drug-induced agent with the position of its listing — 1) Tacrolimus and cyclosporine 2) Ticlopidine and clopidogrel 3) Mitomycin … A) Grouped under calcineurin inhibitors B) Marked 'TTP also' C) The first bullet of the drug list D) Listed under immune-mediated HUS only
questions.exp: The sporadic block lists mitomycin first, then gemcitabine and bevacizumab, then 'Calcineurin inhibitors: tacrolimus, cyclosporine', then ticlopidine and clopidogrel bracketed 'TTP also', and cisplatin; quinine, gemcitabine, quetiapine and cotrimoxazole form the separate immune-mediated list. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: All of the following are printed under the sporadic drug-induced column EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The drug column lists mitomycin, gemcitabine, bevacizumab, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), ticlopidine, clopidogrel and cisplatin; rituximab appears only as post-transplant therapy on p755. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: Gemcitabine appears twice in the causes diagram — once as a sporadic drug-induced agent and once under immune-mediated HUS.
opts: True — and it is also the toxin of streptococcal neuraminidase
True — the same drug is printed in both lists
False — it appears only among calcineurin inhibitors
False — it appears only under immune-mediated HUS
questions.exp: Gemcitabine is the second bullet of 'Sporadic: Drug induced' and the second bullet of 'Immune mediated HUS' on the same page. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Pathophysiology & causes · p754
questions.q: The immune-mediated HUS list contains quinine, gemcitabine, quetiapine and cotrimoxazole; the odd one out from that list is:
questions.exp: Mitomycin sits under sporadic drug-induced causes, not immune-mediated HUS. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Investigation · p754
questions.q: On the peripheral blood smear, schistocytes become significant beyond:
questions.exp: Peripheral blood smear: schistocyte (>2% significant). (Book p754)

questions.sec: Investigation · p754
questions.q: The hemolysis work-up in HUS shows:
opts: Normal LDH, negative Coombs, ↑ direct bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin
↑ LDH, negative Coombs, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin with normal PT/APTT
↑ LDH, positive Coombs, ↓ indirect bilirubin, ↑ haptoglobin
questions.exp: Blood investigation: ↑ LDH, −ve Coombs test, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin level, normal PT/APTT. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Investigation · p754
questions.q: In the coagulation line of the blood investigation block, what is stated as normal?
questions.exp: The blood-investigation list runs: ↑LDH, -ve Coombs test, ↑indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin level, Normal - PT/APTT — normal clotting helps distinguish TMA from DIC. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Investigation · p754
questions.q: Match each column with its complement signature — 1) Atypical HUS pathway 2) SLE pathway 3) Atypical HUS C4 … A) Classical B) Alternative C) Normal
questions.exp: Atypical HUS: alternative pathway, low C3 (N) C4; SLE: classical pathway, low C3 low C4. (Book p754)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: The typical HUS timeline runs: abdominal pain, then 2 days later bloody dysentery (evaluate & start antibiotics), and after 5 more days:
questions.exp: Abdominal pain → 2 days → bloody dysentery → 5 days → 90-95% resolution; 5-10% HUS. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Fill up: In the typical HUS timeline, the bloody dysentery stage carries the instruction 'Evaluate & ______'.
questions.exp: The flow reads: Abdominal pain → 2 days → Bloody dysentery (Evaluate & start antibiotics) → 5 days → 90–95% Resolution or 5–10% HUS. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: How long after the onset of bloody dysentery does the timeline allow before the child resolves or develops HUS?
questions.exp: Two intervals are printed: 2 days from abdominal pain to bloody dysentery, then 5 days from dysentery to the 90–95% resolution versus 5–10% HUS split. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: After the dysentery phase, the proportion that goes on to HUS is:
questions.exp: 90-95% resolution; 5-10% HUS. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: The treatment written for typical HUS is:
questions.exp: Typical HUS treatment: conservative (evaluate & start antibiotics for the dysentery). (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Atypical HUS presents with thrombocytopenia plus features of:
questions.exp: Atypical HUS: features of 2° HTN (renal/endocrine); thrombocytopenia. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: The mainstay of atypical HUS treatment, to be started within 24 hours, is:
questions.exp: PLEX (plasma exchange therapy): within 24 hr; mainstay of treatment. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: In atypical HUS, the costly terminal-complement drug and the immunosuppressant indication written for complement factor H mutation are:
questions.exp: Eculizumab: costly; immunosuppressant in complement factor H mutation; renal transplant listed. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Each of these is a listed treatment line for atypical HUS EXCEPT:
opts: PLEX within 24 hours as the mainstay
Immunosuppressant in complement factor H mutation
questions.exp: The atypical list runs PLEX (within 24hr; mainstay of treatment), eculizumab (costly), immunosuppressant in complement factor H mutation, renal transplant, and recurrence post transplant with rituximab and eculizumab; antibiotics belong to the dysentery stage of typical HUS. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Recurrence of HUS after renal transplant is managed with:
questions.exp: Recurrence post transplant: rituximab; eculizumab. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: In the note table, eculizumab is printed twice — once as a treatment line and once under 'Recurrence post transplant'.
opts: True — recurrence post transplant lists rituximab and eculizumab
False — eculizumab appears only under recurrence
False — the recurrence line names only rituximab
True — and it is also listed under fluids for pre-renal injury
questions.exp: Eculizumab is the second treatment bullet ('Costly') and reappears beneath 'Recurrence post transplant' with rituximab. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Match each feature with its column in the pre-renal vs ATN note — 1) Urine output in pre-renal injury 2) BUN/creatinine in ATN 3) Tubular injury in pre-renal injury … A) < 10:1 B) Normal C) Absent (−)
questions.exp: Pre-renal: normal urine output, − edema, − tubular injury; ATN: decreased output, <10:1 BUN/Cr, + tubular injury. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: The two BUN ratios written side by side in the note table are:
opts: > 20:1 in pre-renal injury vs < 10:1 in ATN
> 10:1 in pre-renal injury vs < 5:1 in ATN
> 30:1 in pre-renal injury vs < 20:1 in ATN
questions.exp: BUN/creatinine: >20:1 pre-renal; <10:1 ATN. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Which statement from the pre-renal vs ATN table is TRUE?
opts: Edema is positive in pre-renal injury
Urine output is decreased in pre-renal injury
Fluids are given in pre-renal injury but withheld in ATN, where edema and tubular injury are positive
Fluids are withheld in pre-renal injury and given in ATN
questions.exp: Pre-renal: fluids given, edema −, tubular injury −; ATN: fluids withhold, edema +, tubular injury +. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Match each row of the note table with what is printed for acute tubular necrosis — 1) Urine output 2) Edema 3) BUN/Creatinine … A) < 10:1 B) Decreased C) + D) −
questions.exp: The necrosis column reads: urine output decreased, edema +, BUN/creatinine < 10:1, fluids withhold, tubular injury +; the pre-renal column carries normal / − / > 20:1 / given / −. (Book p755)

questions.sec: Presentation, treatment & pre-renal vs ATN · p755
questions.q: Fill up: The second column of the note table is headed acute tubular ______, exactly as printed.
questions.exp: The table headers are 'Pre renal injury' and 'Acute tubular necrosis' — this page uses necrosis, whereas p749 expands ATN as acute tubular nephrosis. (Book p755)
